Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to participate in the debate on Bill C-48 at the report stage. It is a bill which seeks to regulate the oil and gas interests in Canada Lands and to amend the Oil and Gas Production and Conservation Act.
I listened with great interest to the comments of the hon. lady, the Minister of State for Mines, the hon. member for Nickel Belt (Mrs. Erola). I found some of her comments were interesting. Speaking as a Nova Scotian, it is obvious to me that she has not been in Nova Scotia lately or she would not have spoken to this House as she did.
The hon. member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson) mentioned that members from Atlantic Canada should address this particular issue. I had an opportunity to speak to this bill at second reading and I welcome this opportunity to place my arguments again before this House. In the time allotted to me I shall attempt to relate my remarks to my native province of Nova Scotia and to the economic impact which this bill, if passed in its present form, would have on our people.
I know the House will understand if I digress for a moment to mention that Nova Scotians who support the Conservative Party are today walking tall as a result of the outcome of the provincial election in my province on October 6. This election showed my party returned to power with 37 seats, while the
Liberals hold only 13, and the NDP, since it elected only one, has lost its status as a party in my province.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext: An interim setback.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext:
One of the NDP members says it is "an interim setback". If you call going backwards almost to anonymity going forward, I guess it all depends on how you read the signs. We are rather pleased with this.
During the campaign our premier asked for a strong mandate so he could take a message to Ottawa indicating that Nova Scotians do not like present federal policies. This, of course, is an understatement. I learned while campaigning with the premier and my provincial colleagues that Nova Scotians at all levels of society are demanding that the federal Liberal government do something about high interest rates, about high mortgage rates, about high rentals, which are now higher than they have ever been in the history of this country; do something about the debased purchasing power of the Canadian dollar and take some action generally to fight the economic problems facing all Canadians.
This bill is related to one of the planks of our premier's program, which is to develop self-reliance in energy for Nova Scotians through resource development. To make this possible we must, of course, have a stronger say in the over-all development of our offshore resources. While of late we could not help but note the more amicable attitude taken by the Right Hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) in finally reaching an agreement between Alberta and Ottawa-which gives us some cause for hope that similar agreements may be reached in Atlantic Canada-there is, however, considerable doubt as to how this will be achieved.
The return to the House of Bill C-48 at this time, when we are faced with so many other problems in this nation, only serves to reinforce these doubts about the government's intentions. In my opinion this bill is obviously improperly worded and should be withdrawn completely from this House.
When the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources introduced this bill to the House on December 11, 1980, he called it the key element in the successful fullfilment of the government's national energy program. He waxed eloquent as he stated that our offshore regions cover an area of some 2.5 million square miles. The territories alone, he said comprise another 1.5 million square miles. Together this is what the Liberal Party calls the Canada lands, an area which is almost twice the size of the ten provinces combines.
The minister claimed that oil and gas rights have already been issued for 350 million acres in the Canada lands and that the bill will convert existing rights to the land management regime establishing it in a meaningful way. This same minister, when speaking at the report stage of Bill C-48, added insult to injury so far as we in Atlantic Canada are concerned when, as reported at page 11472 of Hansard of July 13, he stated;
October 14, 1981

When the resources belong to the people of Canada, would it be responsible to have a situation where the premiers or heads of various governments could veto development?
In the next paragraph he stated:
The notion that a particular region of this country could prevent the people of Canada from getting the benefit of resources which belong to them is one which we as a government cannot accept.
These words are fighting words thrown in the face of Atlantic Canada's premiers. I ask this house: by what authority does this government and the federal Liberal Party say that the resources off Atlantic Canada's coast belong to all the people of Canada? Maybe the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Rompkey) can answer that question. I would like to hear him expound on this particular thesis.
As Nova Scotians we have based our claim to these resources as far back as 1621 when King James I granted the Royal Charter of Nova Scotia to Sir William Alexander. At that time, in recognition of the utter dependence of the colonies on the sea as a means of transport, he granted as well the water adjacent to our shores to the provinces. In recognition of this dependence, the king included as part of our territory a band of sea stretching about 100 miles seaward from our coast. This particular band easily encompasses Sable Island and covers a large section of the grey area, the controversial Georges Bank, and it also covers a large section of what we call the Scotian shelf.
These boundaries were observed for many years despite numerous conquests and treaty settlements. In fact, Canada's Constitution, the British North America Act of 1867, provided that Nova Scotia's limits would be exactly the same after confederation as they were before.
This claim is further supported by a parliamentary document entitled "Offshore Mineral Resources, Legal Aspects", which says at page 2:
At Confederation, Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Quebec and Ontario retained ownership of the "lands, mines, minerals and royalties", and all public property then belonging to them.
This was embodied respectively in Sections 109 and 117 of the British North America Act. This proviso was also made applicable to Prince Edward Island and British Columbia when they joined Canada. In the western provinces the situation differed initially, as the natural resources were reserved to the federal government when Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba were carved out of what was then called Rupert's Land.
However, the British North America Act of 1930 subsequently transferred the same rights to those provinces, and when Newfoundland became part of Canada in 1949 it was put in a similar position by term 37 of the Terms of Union. Thus, I point out to the House, there is historical and legal justification for provincial resource ownership. This is why I suggest Bill C-48 should be withdrawn. It should be reconsidered and its wording should be changed so its enactment in its present form will not rape, rob, pillage and plunder an area which has too long been classified as a have-not area.
Canada Oil and Gas Act
We have worked hard in Atlantic Canada, especially in Nova Scotia, to literally pull ourselves up by our bootstraps. Now that we have clearly established and reaffirmed the provincial right to control land-based resources, as is clearly written into the British North America Act, the claim of the Atlantic provinces to rights covering undersea oil and gas resources off our shores can surely no longer be denied us Nova Scotians, in my view. Now more than ever before there is legitimacy in the argument long held by Nova Scotians that the undersea resources should be deeded to those of us who live in Atlantic Canada in compensation for the mineral-rich lands which other provinces have received early in this century. The Atlantic region has far too long been ignored in its request to be given the same consideration which the federal government gave other provinces through the provision of land where great treasure has been found. Land which, incidentally, all provinces originally held in joint ownership. I feel very strongly about this issue or I would not have taken the time and the effort to speak twice on this same measure.
We do not want the federal government to give us anything to which we are not entitled. We are not beggars and we are not begging, but neither do we want the federal government to take away from us those lands and resources which we feel, we know, and we believe we legitimately own in law under the terms of Bill C-48.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext:
Those are our lands. In the pirit of justice, fairness and equality, Sir, and in compensation for having surrendered our claims to the northern lands given other provinces, the day has surely arrived when our federal government should no longer hold us in bondage, making us come like a beggar hat in hand here to Ottawa looking for crumbs. It should make up for the oversights of the past and enlarge our territories by recognizing that the land under the sea, to the limits of exploitability, belong to us. We would thereby find our place in the sun.
I can assure you, Sir, that we will be like other provinces. We will be willing to share, but we feel we must have the opportunity throughout the eighties and the nineties to make Nova Scotia self-reliant. In simple language, we must be able to pay our own way. That is all we are asking.
The oil and gas finds off the east coast are promising, exciting and, I believe, they are substantial. Their development can provide us with revenues, lower cost fuels and a competitive source of power for homes and industry. We as Nova Scotians must be assured that supportive industries that foster oil development under the North Atlantic, that support and maintain drilling and the eventual production of raw fuels, are based in Nova Scotia or in Newfoudland, as much as possible. There will be plenty for both our provinces and we want to have a say.
We have been looking for the light at the end of the tunnel for years, Mr. Speaker. Now light is slowly dawning. New

October 14, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
opportunities are being thrust upon us. We feel we have to be ready to meet the challenge and to provide trained, willing and eager Nova Scotians to profit from the job opportunities opening up.
1 urge the House again to withdraw this bill at this time because the timing is wrong. If it passes in its present form, what does it do? It places not just a little club but a very big club in the hands of the Right Hon. Prime Minister. It makes a mockery of the proposals put forth by that hon. gentleman to the Premier of Nova Scotia on July 21. In that letter, the Prime Minister stated that he shared Premier Buchanan's view about the desirability of beginning to devise co-operative administrative arrangements and a system of revenue-sharing which will prove acceptable to the two levels of government.
Said the Prime Minister in the second paragraph:
This issue cannot remain unresolved much longer. It is therefore the intention of the federal government to see the matter resolved through the legal process while federal-provincial discussions concentrate on the more germane aspects of administrative mechanisms and revenue-sharing.
In the third paragraph, the Prime Minister states:
In this context, 1 would like to propose that we undertake an intensive round of negotiations this fall with a view to resolving all outstanding matters by February, 1982. If by then we have not reached an agreement, we should await the outcome of the legal process, which would of course mean that any future negotiations would start from a different base.
Mr. Speaker, that is the big club we would be giving the right hon. gentleman if we passed this bill now. If we used the right hon. gentleman's own reasoning, there should be no further debate on this bill, in fairness to Premier Buchanan and in fairness to Premier Peckford of Newfoundland, until February of 1982. This could mean that, pending the outcome of the negotiations and the legal process, the discussions could then start from an entirely new base. Those were the Prime Minister's own words.
I submit, Mr. Speaker, that the stakes are very high for Atlantic Canada. They are too high for us and for the federal government to rush in at this moment to try to settle this matter in a hurry.
I am pleased to see the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. De Bane) in the House since I wish to quote briefly from his own document. The hon. gentleman, in Volume No. 1 of his magazine Evolution, states, on page 11, that the onshore impact of offshore activity could produce 20,000 to, 30,000 direct jobs, some 150,000 indirect jobs, and investment could reach $8 billion. The article goes on to list the fields in which this activity would take place, such as temporary and permanent service bases, repair, maintenance and steel platform fabrication yards, pipeline installation and pipeline coating yards, partial processing facilities, gas processing and treatment plants and marine terminals. I am only listing a few of the possible golden opportunities that await those of us who live in Atlantic Canada. All these are quoted in the booklet put out by the hon. Minister of Regional Economic Expansion.
It is for these reasons, Mr. Speaker, that Nova Scotians and citizens of Atlantic Canada are going to fight. We are going to
fight hard for our rightful place when administrative arrangements and revenue-sharing decisions are made by government authorities. It is unfortunate, Mr. Speaker, that this government did not give more time to resolving the difficulties we face owing to the breakdown of the Law of the Sea Conference instead of concentrating its efforts on Bill C-48. When the 150-nation UN conference adjourned this summer in Geneva, the Times of London summarized its results as follows:
The old regime has not been cast aside and cannot yet be, although its days are numbered. The new order is almost ready, and is waiting to take its place, but it cannot yet occupy the centre of the stage.
The bombshell was dropped at that conference by United States Ambassador James Malone when he said:
The political and economic interests of the United States need to be better protected in the decision-making system of the proposed international seabed authority.
This causes me to ask, where does the breakdown of this conference leave Canada and Canadians? Most of what we have obtained so far in maritime terms beyond the old three-mile limit has been obtained only by unilateral declaration. They include the economic zone. While the 200-mile fishing zone may be safe, I submit to this House that the 200-mile mining and drilling zone is definitely in jeopardy. We claim- only by unilateral declaration-sovereignty over the Arctic archipelago, the waters in between, and the Arctic islands. We claim-only by unilateral declaration-national jurisdiction over the continental shelf and its resources, principally petroleum. None of these declared assertions of jurisdiction will be recognized internationally if the Law of the Sea convention is not concluded and ratified.
Since we are unable to defend our claims with armed force, there may well be invasions of our proclaimed sovereign areas by those who want to drill for oil within the 200-mile limit or drag for minerals on our continental shelf, unless the convention becomes accepted international law.
What we do have under the 1958 international convention on the continental shelf is jurisdiction on the seabed and in the subsoil out to the limits of exploitability, which today means about 1000 feet. On the east coast, this barely covers Hibernia. Prime Minister failed to convince President Reagan, for example, that the Law of the Sea was an important item both for Ottawa and the North-South Summit at which, I understand, it was not discussed. Mr. Speaker, I had not intended to speak this afternoon, but both the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson) and the hon. member for South Shore (Mr. Crouse) have referred to me, and I feel, moreover, that it is important to put the facts on the record, in view of the allegations and positions put forward by the opposition.
The main case the opposition is putting forward is ownership. Ownership is completely irrelevant in this issue. Hon. members opposite are arguing on the grounds put forward by the Premier of Newfoundland. When the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Clark) was head of the administration, he wrote a letter to the Premier of Newfoundland. If the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre had gone on to quote the letter at greater length than he did, I think he would have shown that that letter was so full of holes as to be meaningless. The then prime minister granted ownership on certain conditions, and those conditions certainly depended on federal jurisdiction. In my opinion, that letter from the then prime minister was really not worth the paper on which it was written and, indeed, did not address in a legitimate way the question of ownership because that issue cannot be addressed.
Ownership is not the relevant issue, and I think we should put t'hat to rest. Let me give an example. The province of Newfoundland owns the forests of Newfoundland, it owns every tree in Newfoundland, yet we have signed three DREE agreements with that province to improve the forest industry there and to build up the provincial forest service. There is no way it could have been done without federal participation. That resource is completely and utterly owned by the province, but I submit it would have been impossible to develop the forests of Newfoundland without federal participation. The question of ownership in that case is completely and utterly irrelevant.
Let me give a second example. A mine in my riding is being closed down. It is not a question of ownership. The province owns that mine, it owns all the minerals under the earth, yet where is the province coming for help? It is coming to the federal government.
I submit again that ownership is not the relevant issue. Just because you own something that does not mean you have jurisdiction over it or you control it because the important concept here is not ownership at all but, indeed, jurisdiction and control, and that is what we have been trying to point out to the Government of Newfoundland for the last two years.

Canada Oil and Gas Act
Now it seems that the Government of Newfoundland is starting to see the light. We have not changed our position at all, but the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) had to go to Newfoundland to clarify that position on television in order to get the provincial government to start to negotiate, hopefully in good faith. The principle we have been stating ever since the 1979 election-and that position has not changed at all-is that we want to negotiate with the province of Newfoundland and, indeed, with the other maritime provinces on the basis of revenue sharing and jurisdiction. We have said consistently that 100 per cent of the provincial-type revenues would go to the provinces as if the resources were onshore. The Prime Minister has quite clearly said that whatever revenues the provinces would normally get would go to them as if the resources were onshore. I do not think it can be made much clearer than that. That, it seems to me, is very clear. Revenues would be treated as if the resources were onshore and as if the provinces indeed were controlling those resources onshore.
[DOT] (WOO)
The second thing we have offered is joint jurisdiction. We have said that it should not be the provincial government alone or the federal government alone, but indeed the federal jurisdiction applying concurrently its jurisdiction to that problem.
The people of every province in this country, particularly Nova Scotia and Newfoundland, are very fortunate because they do not have only one government working for them, they have two. Some people in my province have been asking me for the past two years to choose between being a Newfoundlander and being a Canadian. I refuse to make that choice. I am proud to be a resident of that province and at the same time proud to be a Canadian.
1 reject those who ask me to make a choice. I will not make that choice. That is the essence of Canadianism. The people of Newfoundland are fortunate, and they know they are fortunate to have not one but two governments acting on their behalf. That is what we are saying.
Surely the federal jurisdiction and the provincial jurisdiction together are more important, powerful and effective in the long run than both governments working separately or indeed, even worse, both working at loggerheads. That is what we are proposing. Hopefully, if we can get the provinces to focus on the issues and negotiate in good faith, we can have an agreement, one that is good for Newfoundland.
I agree with my colleague from South Shore that we need those revenues, not handouts or dependence. We want real jobs and real money coming from those jobs for resource development. I agree with that. All Newfoundlanders want to see that.
The only way to do that is to get a deal that will be good for Newfoundland and good for Canada. Here is the importance of Bill C-48. While Newfoundland has a very real need that we can and must address to the resolution of these negotiations, Canada has a need as well. Those resources off the east coast of Canada are just as important as the resources in the Beaufort Sea and the resources in Alberta.
Until we can have a package, program and policy that encompasses, uses and plans the development of all those resources jointly, we will not be able to solve the energy problem in this country and have a great impact on the more serious problem of inflation.
We are fortunate, we can achieve self-sufficiency in Canada. However, there is a Canadian need now and we must address it. We in Newfoundland have to see not only to our own need, which is very real and urgent. We can solve that and it must be solved. We can have money going into Newfoundland. If the province of Newfoundland had started negotiating two years ago as it is doing today, we could have had a deal. Those revenues, which are sorely needed, would be going into that province.
The other consideration is the Canadian need. That must be addressed. The question of ownership is not the relevant issue. Who owns what is immaterial. It can be put aside. Who gets the money, who has the jurisdiction and control are the relevant issues. Those are the matters we should be talking about, not spurious, irrelevant issues that really do not matter in the long run.
Now that the negotiations are going on, now that the Government of Newfoundland and indeed the Government of Nova Scotia have come around to seeing that we must negotiate along those lines, I hope we can have an agreement and will create those jobs which are very necessary in eastern Canada.

subsubtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING OIL AND GAS INTERESTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in addressing myself to motions Nos. 4 and 51,1 think I will take some liberty in dealing with the other five motions as well because we may not have another opportunity to speak to them.
The environmental resolutions which have been grouped for debate by Madam Speaker show how inadequate this legislation is when it comes to the protection of the environment. The lack of concern for the environment is demonstrated by the government very clearly. The environmental provisions of this bill are equal only to the contempt the government has shown to people north of 60 when introducing the new regime for oil and gas exploration.
Members will remember that the committee which was studying this legislation supported a unanimous motion to travel north of 60 and how the Liberals came to the next meeting, packed it with members who were not present when the first motion to travel was passed, and rescinded it. That kind of activity became the trademark of the behaviour of Liberal committee members. What is the fear on the government's side about travelling north of 60? Are they afraid to find out the truth, that Bill C-48 is in fact a blueprint for the interests of Canadians south of 60 and has not achieved the bare minimum to protect culture and environment in the north?
The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) has a hyped-up sales pitch that Bill C-48 will play a vital role in Canadianizing the oil and gas industry. The environment is disturbed just as much regardless of who owns the machinery. The important issue is the regulatory regime. Ducks disturbed by aircraft and polar bears slicked with oil have little concern about whose pockets are Filling fastest from the exploitation.
What is important to the biological environment is a system of checks and balances that demands of industry the most benign form of interaction possible. The sneaky reversal of the committee's plan to travel was equalled at a later date when the Liberals and my Tory friends on the right made a sweetheart deal to close off debate on the bill while it was still in
committee. Anyone familiar with parliamentary procedure knows that the reason we are debating this bill now is that the Liberals and Tories are in the same sticky swamp and that report stage debate was taking place because the Conservatives went into the deal with the Liberals with a few parliamentary screws loose.
It is clear, Mr. Speaker, that Bill C-48 is designed to speed up the exploration for oil and gas on what have been called Canada lands. That in itself may be laudable from a narrow supply point of view, but with the lack of environmental provisions in the legislation I am afraid we are looking at an environmental disaster in the making.
How can proper baseline data be collected when the permit structure is of such an accelerated design? Important biological studies will never be done for several reasons. First, the legislation is designed to speed up oil and gas exploration without any balancing mechanism to protect plants or animals, and second, the legislation is purposely drafted to avoid dealing with environmental impact costs.
It is therefore inevitable that many species will be unduly disrupted, damaged and in some instances completely destroyed. Bill C-48 is written with such a singular vision and preoccupation-to extract oil and gas-that even the proposed role for the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) has been sidelined.
Bill C-48 is much like a court composed of a prosecutor only. The minister has opted for all the powers of decision despite the obvious conflict of interest.
Let me first deal with what I think is the major fault of this legislation regarding the environment. Some of my colleagues have talked about the other silent partners in this legislation- the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro) and the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans (Mr. LeBlanc)-however, the minister who sits most idly while his department is bypassed by the monolithic energy department is the Minister of the Environment.
At the March 12, 1981, meeting of the Fisheries and Forestry Committee, I asked the minister about some of the environmental concerns passed on to us by groups such as CARC, the West Coast Environmental Law Association, the United Fishermen and Allied Workers Union and many other groups. Besides referring a question about staff requirements to his departmental officials, the minister said that he was "happy to have this kind of question because, as minister, I never feel that my colleagues give me quite as much in the way of resources as I need to undertake the important work of the north".
That statement, Mr. Speaker, is shocking. It shows just how little the Minister of the Environment knows about Bill C-48. If the minister does not do anything about his participation in Bill C-48, he will be standing with one toe in a lake killed by acid rain but up to his neck in oil slicks and tales of the demise of Canada's wildlife resources.
October 14, 1981

Why are we concerned about the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and particularly this minister, when it comes to the environment? Let us look at the record of the Department of .Energy, Mines and Resources and its track record with the environment.
The Minister of the Environment should read some of the reports produced by his own department. A report prepared in April of last year documents the concerns senior departmental officials have about offshore exploration and the problems they have in relation to the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources.
Perhaps the most condemning comment is found on page 13 of the report which reads: "The lack of environmental consciousness exhibited by EMR is a concern." I regard this as a tough statement for public servants to make. This is a comment from a government official, not a member of the opposition. It is clear that EMR is a proponent department. A proponent department like EMR is by mandate and definition primarily, if not totally, concerned with getting oil and gas out of the ground and from under the water. Mr. Speaker, that is expected of them. But there is a need for adequate checks and balances, and these are not present in Bill C-48. I say and the NDP says that the proper check on EMR's mad dash for oil and gas should rest with the Department of the Environment.
No moves have been made to give formal protective status to the 150 or more identified and internationally recognized ecological sites north of 60. There are still only six federal wildlife biologists north of 60. There have been no settlements of claim with Canada's first Canadians north of 60-to protect and enhance their culture and traditional interaction with wildlife and the environment.
Bill C-48 is, I am sure, epic poetry-music to the cash register ears for which it is written, but Bill C-48 is an obituary to many cultures and species.
The report I referred to earlier goes on as follows: "The Department of the Environment should act as spokesman in respect of environment, identifying to and for the government, environmental concerns." We know Mr. Speaker, that the proposed national resources management administration which I understand will be announced next week by the government, will include representatives from the Department of Fisheries and Oceans, the Department of the Environment and others, but we also know who pushes whom around in this government and in other governments. I predict, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister of the Environment and the Minister of Fisheries and Oceans will gather a lot of dust in this arrangement. 1 challenge the government to publish the minutes of the meetings of this council. That way, we will see whose interests are being protected and whose interests are being raised.
In fact, on June 18, 1981 in committee, the minister said he would release the terms of reference of the council. Because of the Liberal-Tory deal to close debate in committee, however, we do not have those guidelines. I would ask the minister to table those terms of reference in the House during this debate.
Canada Oil and Gas Act
Mr. Speaker, the minister's proposed council is not laid out in the legislation and I would like to raise a few points about why it should be if it is relevant to the amendments before us.
One of the criticisms of the federal government's environmental assessment procedure is that it is not enshrined in legislation. I have expressed my concerns about this matter, and 1 would certainly want improvements in the assessment process before it is legislated. 1 should like to refer to a number of reports that show why the lack of a legislative mandate to protect the environment in Bill C-48 is such a bad move by the government.
A report done in December 1978 by the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources says that there has been "slow acceptance at senior levels of the long-term need to make environmental evaluation a basic element in both the economic analysis and planning processes." In layman's language that means that senior people in the department are not particularly concerned about the environment. The report refers to the environmental assessment and review process as it relates to the department.
The report also says there are problems in EMR in implementing the necessary processes. This point was pursued by the Canadian Arctic Resources Committee. In a letter to members of the committee studying Bill C-48, it expressed serious concerns about the lack of staff in EMR to carry out minimal environmental research.
The Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development-the silent partner-is no better. Despite the fact that EARP was established by cabinet in December, 1973, by December 1980 the department had still not established procedures on environmental screening-after over eight years. A recent article in the Ottawa Citizen makes reference to pressure being exerted on the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development to grant exploratory rights before legislation recognizing native rights is passed by Parliament. The government's hypocrisy is shown by its intention to proceed with the Norman Wells pipeline despite the completely unchallenged work of Mr. Justice Thomas Berger.

speechtext:
They have been running around the country saying that Bill C-48 is "neutral" on land claims, but when pressed to come up with a legal opinion we see what a charade the government parades as the truth.
At this point I want to remind the noisy member opposite that the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development agreed on June 1 to provide a legal opinion on whether Bill C-48 affects land claims negotiations. He promised that when native people were present at committee. To date we have not seen that opinion. In fact, the minister has written to me

October 14, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
indicating that he does not intend to provide any legal opinion. One could well assume that Bill C-48 has much worse implications for the resolution of aboriginal title and rights than was previously thought. Again, it is the Liberal gain-promise everything when the TV lights are on but in the cool mushroom atmosphere of cabinet privacy, sing a different tune.
It is clear, Mr. Speaker, that the environment will take the back seat on this legislation and our party will continue to argue for recognition of the need to protect the environment from Liberal abuse, and Canadians from Liberal deception.
Mr. Speaker, the amendments proposed by the hon. member for Nunatsiaq (Mr. Ittinuar) and myself recognize the importance of the environment and would give the government and all Canadians a mandate to protect the delicate ecology of the north and the offshore, both in British Columbia and in Atlantic Canada.
Having documented the concerns our party has over the feeble position of the Minister of the Environment on this bill, I would like to make some points on the specific amendments presently before the House.
Our motion to define a spill as "an amount of 100 litres or more of oil and any other substance deemed foreign to the environment" will give the government a legislative mandate to control chronic oil pollution, which, as my colleague the hon. member for Nanaimo-Alberni (Mr. Miller) has pointed out, could present us with more long-term environmental problems than even major oil spills that rigs like Ixtoc in the Gulf of Mexico last year caused.
On June 6, 1981, the minister had this to say about my definition for quantifying a spill:
We would rather leave it open, and then if we want to act on a one-litre spill, we can act on a one-litre spill.
I do not know if the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources thinks that statement fools anyone. If 100 litres is too big, then 1 will stand aside-and I am confident my colleague, the hon. member for Nunatsiaq will also do so-for a further amendment taking it from 100 litres down to one litre. I will support the minister's own proposal of one litre; but let us see a quantifiable legal definition.
I just want to quote from a report written by Environment Canada in June, 1978, that says:
-the cumulative effects of small leaks and spills over long periods of time are capable of devastating salt marshes, fish spawning areas, shellfish areas, etc.
Let us look at the experience elsewhere. In Wales, the harbour authority has defined a spill as anything over a few barrels. What this has done is to give a mandate to the local authorities to watch the chronic oil pollution problem closely, but it has also meant that the companies involved have taken the time to train their employees properly and have recognized the importance of controlling these kinds of spills. Incidentally, when a quantified level was set, the spill rate in Wales dropped to one spill in 100 from previous levels.
In committee, the minister would not release the proposed regulations that he says would govern a spill. In fact, when he was asked by another of my colleagues if he might define a spill as 10,000 gallons, he said he might make exceptions such as in the regulations. That is just not good enough. If the minister thinks 100 litres is too big and one litre is about right, but that 10,000 gallons is okay, I think it is clear, in the interests of clarifying this for the minister himself, that we should have a quantifiable level spelled out in this legislation.
Our next motion, No. 51, seeks to amend Bill C-48 by including "authorized" spills under the environmental sections of the bill. Undoubtedly there will be authorized spills, such as the Baffin Island oil spill project, which we have already seen, where studies are being done to assess whether chemical dispersants will be effective in dealing with oil spilled in the Arctic, and also to determine the impact of oil in the Arctic environment. However, to exclude these spills from the environmental sections of Bill C-48 or other bills is wrong.
For example, we all remember the disastrous oil spill test of last year. We assume it was authorized last year when polar bears were used in a test and two of them died as a result of being covered in oil. That is perhaps an acceptable experiment from a biological point of view, but the damage to the ecology even from authorized spills may be serious enough that the liability and other provisions of this legislation must cover them, as well.
Once again, the minister will say it is in the regulations. This is a minor change that will show that the government is, in fact, concerned about the environment. I urge the government members to include authorized spills under the general environmental aspects of Bill C-48.
Motion 52, which we are presently considering, seeks to broaden the provisions of this section by giving advance notice to people who are affected. That is important in light of my earlier comments regarding the need for the public to know about this government's intentions regarding environmental pollution by companies.
Motion 53, which is presented by my colleague from Nunatsiaq broadens the provisions for liability. It is clear that should oil and gas exploration proceed as outlined under Bill C-48, and with the inevitability of a spill, there must be adequate protection of those people whose livelihood will be destroyed or drastically altered. To the fishermen on both coasts and to the aboriginal people in the north who will be affected most dramatically by a speed-up in exploration, this amendment will offer some minimal amount of protection.
There will be massive exploration carried out under this new regime. There is no doubt about that. The people who will bear the brunt must have assurances that their livelihood will be protected. The government's proposals do not go far enough and must be changed.
I hope to deal with Madam Speaker's ruling on Motion 54 at another time; however, let me say that Beauchesne's Section 7 of Citation 773 does not apply because Motion No. 54 does not place any charge upon the public treasury. Motion 56 is
October 14, 1981

closely related to Motion No. 53. We are proposing this particular amendment because of the need to recognize problems associated with identifying the time when a compensation period can start.
In order to illustrate this I would like to cite a few examples. We are faced here with the possibility of damage to a person's livelihood as the result of an oil spill. For example, an oil spill may occur, go unreported and disappear from view, as did much of the oil in the Gulf of Mexico with the Ixtoc spill where it mixed with the water column. It will then resurface at some time later to foul the fishermen's nets, a boat, a shore, a bird-nesting area, or whatever. Under the present legislation, fishermen or other individuals would have a severely limited opportunity to pursue compensation.
I also want to mention briefly a parallel case. The Canadian Environmental Law Association has presented the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources with proposed changes to the Nuclear Liability Act. Their purpose is to see changes to the legislation that would enable victims of radiation exposure to claim at a later date. As members know, people who work in the nuclear field may develop cancer which only becomes apparent long after exposure. The limitation period in the Nuclear Liability Act should be changed to allow for compensation claims at a later date. It is under the same principle that I feel Bill C-48 should be changed.
Motion 57, which we have also moved, calls on the government to conduct an inquiry when there has been a spill or an accident caused by an operator who is acting under this legislation. It is clear that in the case of a spill, the minister should order an inquiry. How better to learn and avoid repetition? To be honest, I do not trust any government nor should it be left to a minister's discretion, such as is proposed in Bill C-48. An inquiry must take place.
I sat in committee during almost all the meetings at which Bill C-48 was considered. We heard evidence from a number of environmental groups, and all of them pointed out the serious deficiencies of this bill when it comes to consideration of the environment. The NDP fought in committee to present amendments, and we will continue to fight for the amendments which we have proposed.
Let me conclude by saying that no witnesses appeared before the committee to propose that there be no environmental regime, which is what Bill C-48 contains at present under the existing regime put forward by the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, under normal circumstances, one might express pleasure at participating in this debate during the report stage of Bill C-48. It is a most important piece of legislation which will set the rules for all future gas and oil exploration and development on Crown lands. But there can be little pleasure-certainly little pleasure for me as one member-in being associated with what is actually a sham. Sir, I say "sham" with some care and advisedly because the government is only pretending to consid-
Canada Oil and Gas Act
er the views of Members of Parliament and the public in connection with Bill C-48. Although true of the bill as a whole, that is especially true of the environmental dimensions, including the seven motions coupled for debate today.
Bill C-48 was devised to accomplish a number of things. Its stated and ostensible purpose-its purpose for public consumption-is to introduce a new oil and gas exploration and development regime for federal lands in the north and offshore areas. The legislation is central certainly to the government's National Energy Program and therefore to its grand design to Canadianize the petroleum industry. The government's hidden agenda, however, is to proclaim the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Lalonde) as the energy czar for all of Canada, with powers that not only undermine the private sector but also usurp the responsibilities of other cabinet ministers.
Motions Nos. 4, 51, 52, 53, 55, 56 and 57 inaugurate Parliament s consideration of the environmental provisions of Bill C-48 at the report stage. In addition to the seven motions we are debating now, many other motions on the environment will be debated, including ones that I and my colleagues in the Progressive Conservative Party are sponsoring. But probably few of these motions, maybe not even one, stand a ghost of a chance of passing, for the government has steadfastly refused from the beginning to depart from the narrow course it has set for itself. Doubtless the minister will ensure that the trained seals in the Liberal caucus will vote to impose this set of far-reaching rules and regulations for energy development on a land mass greater than all the ten provinces combined. Judging from their supine performance and track record in the standing committee, the same yes-men will neither understand nor care about the profoundly harmful consequences the bill will have for the country as a whole.
A measure of how determined the minister is to get his own way is the fact that not one of the dozens of recommendations made by the Department of Fisheries and Oceans for changes in the bill has been accepted. Concerns expressed by the Department of the Environment have also been ignored, as have those of the government's own independent advisory bodies, for example, the Environmental Advisory Council. The Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) himself was not, to my knowledge, invited to appear as a witness before the Commons Standing Committee on National Resources and Public Works which dealt with the bill, nor have non-government environmental organizations fared any better.
It is bad enough that the Minister of the Environment has been ignored, but so have reputable organizations which made excellent representations at the committee stage. Their views were dismissed out of hand by the government. Is it any wonder then that we in the opposition have had little success in having Bill C-48 changed to reflect sound environmental principles?
Some of the specific environmental concerns expressed about the bill are embodied in the seven motions currently

October 14, 1981
Canada Oil and Gas Act
being debated as a group in the House today, tomorrow and, we hope, Friday and beyond. Other motions not yet before the House, including some of my own, are more fundamental. One in particular, strikes at the heart of what is wrong with the bill from an environmental point of view. I am referring to the amendment proposed by me in committee and now put forward as Motion No. 36 in the name of the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre (Mr. Wilson). The motion would delegate to the Minister of the Environment responsibility for administering the major environmental provisions of the bill. As the legislation stands, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and, to a lesser extent, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Munro), are delegated that responsibility.
I realize that we are not debating Motion No. 36 today but I want to discuss the seven that we are debating in the context of other motions. Without such an approach I do not think a full understanding would be possible. As the legislation stands, the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources and, to a lesser extent, the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development have delegated to them the main environmental responsibility under Bill C-48. As my colleague, the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) has pointed out, that fact makes a mockery of environmental principles because those two ministers have the strongest vested interest in energy development. They should thus be the last ones asked to protect the environment from the very activities they themselves have a mandate to promote. The problem was recognized in the 1970 throne speech of a government preceding the existing one. In part, that throne speech reads:
There is an inherent conflict of interest... between those who are seeking exploitation of non-renewable resources and those who are charged with the responsibility of protecting the environment.
Bill C-48 violates the principle that proponent departments in the energy field should not be the custodians of the environment in the face of activities in which they have a direct interest. Otherwise, it would be like hiring the town arsonist to be fire chief.
My comments apply especially to Clause 49, which we are seeking to amend this session. It would establish a multimil-lion-dollar environmental studies fund to be controlled not by the Minister of the Environment but, rather, by the Minister of Energy, for south of 60 and by the Minister of Northern Development for north of 60. The fund is supposed to finance studies of a broad, baseline nature so as to ensure that resource activities on Crown lands respect both the environment and the lifestyle of the native peoples and other residents
in the areas affected. But because ministers of proponent departments, namely the two I have mentioned, will administer the fund rather than the Minister of the Environment- who is by definition a disinterested party, somebody without a vested interest in the developments which may well threaten the environment-fishermen, native peoples and coastal residents, will have to go begging, cap in hand, to the minister of energy and to the minister of northern affairs for environmental studies, to be carried out. How can anyone be confident that either minister will respond objectively to requests for environmental studies when the resultant findings might document the wisdom of halting pet projects of those two ministers?
In my view it is essential that the minister responsible for the protection of the environment have an arm's length relationship to projects that might threaten the environment. Bill C-48 violates that principle in spades.
During the committee stage of Bill C-48, the minister of energy, his officials, and his parliamentary secretary, whom 1 see on the other side of the chamber today, stressed that co-ordinating mechanisms would be established to ensure that the Department of the Environment would be consulted on all environmental matters related to resource development on Crown lands. But I ask again, why has the Minister of the Environment been given the secondary role in what is essentially an environmental area? The government has the cart before the horse. In this context, it is the minister of energy who should be consulted by the Minister of the Environment, not the other way around.
We are taking enormous risks with the future of Canada if we do not build proper environmental safeguards into any regime for resource development in the frontier areas of our great dominion. When I say that, I am referring to the Arctic and the maritime offshore. The Arctic alone covers some 40 per cent of the territory of our entire country. Although vast, it is the most environmentally vulnerable of all regions. Because of the frigid climate, a major oil spill or well-site blow-out in the Arctic could spell disaster for the delicate ecosystem and for the traditional lifestyle of the native peoples who depend on it for survival. We cannot afford the luxury of waiting until after the damage is done to take action because, according to experts, the damage may well be irreversible.
May I call it six o'clock, Mr. Speaker?
